World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Premier says algal bloom 'gone' despite expansion of fishing restrictions
World.content:
Despite a government declaration that "the algal bloom is gone" from almost all of the state's coast, restrictions on fishing will be strengthened from Friday because of its devastating impact on some stocks.

Fishers have previously expressed grave doubts about the longevity of stocks in gulf waters, with some urging the government to indefinitely close the state's two major gulfs to catches, fearing a total wipe-out of certain species.

SA fishers demand urgent action to protect stocks Easter is a popular time for consumers to purchase fish, but commercial fishers in South Australia say stocks have been decimated by the algal bloom. They fear it will get worse without further action.

The state government has now announced additional restrictions from May 1, including on garfish, King George whiting and southern calamari, with a "total closure" to apply to calamari catches in both the Gulf St Vincent and Spencer Gulf.

But the government also signalled its response to the bloom was shifting to a recovery phase, with Premier Peter Malinauskas stating the bloom had "essentially cleared up" and that for weeks there had been "effectively zero Karenia throughout the state's coastline".

He said various measures introduced in response to the bloom would be scaled back — including water testing, the frequency of updates on the Beachsafe app and the resourcing of the algal bloom hotline, as well as coastal clean-up, which has been conducted by crews patrolling beaches and removing dead fish.

"We've gone from collecting something like 9,500 kilos a week of dead marine life to now less than 50," Mr Malinauskas said.

Countless numbers of dead marine life washed up on SA shores in the months after March 2025. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"We are not seeing [it] arriving on our shores anything like what we saw at the height of the bloom … so now is the time of course to wind back those efforts.

"The regular drumbeat of weekly testing in our metropolitan and other locations across the state will go to a monthly regime of testing, which is more appropriate given the circumstances we now find ourselves in."

Signs warning of the bloom along the coast will also be removed when beaches record four consecutive weeks of either no or low levels of algae, the government said.

A sign at Somerton along Adelaide's coast advising beachgoers in August. (ABC News: Isabel Dayman)

The government said that of the more than 110 onshore testing sites, all but one — Bickers Island off southern Eyre Peninsula — recorded "zero or low levels" of Karenia in recent testing.

But marine scientist and executive director of the South Australian Research and Development Institute (SARDI) Mike Steer said authorities would continue to investigate the environmental impact.

"The job is not done," Professor Steer said.

What public wasn't told about SA toxic algal bloom The government knew a harmful toxin had been found in its algal bloom, but took months to update its health advice.

"We've learnt a lot over the past year and there's still some research gaps that need to be filled to ensure that South Australia remains prepared in case this flares up again."

Similarly, Mr Malinauskas said the bloom's decline could not be taken for granted, and that while algal monitoring would be reduced, it would still be ongoing.

"Is it good news that the algal bloom is gone? Of course it is," he said.

"The coast is effectively clear.

"The algal bloom has essentially cleared up and not been with us for a long time [but] it's also true that it might come back, which is exactly why we've got to continue to invest in the monitoring and the research efforts."

Mike Steer says authorities would continue to investigate the environmental impact from the algal bloom. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Greens MP Robert Simms — who chaired a parliamentary inquiry into the bloom — said he hoped the repeal of elements of the government's summer plan, announced in October, would not lead to cuts in available financial support.

"There should be certainty provided to everybody in the community around how the government is handling the algal bloom," he said.

"One of the things that came out in the parliamentary inquiry was that there were significant gaps in water testing in the lead-up to the algal bloom first being detected … [and] we need to ensure going forward that there's a consistent pattern and approach being taken to testing."

Mr Simms said there had been no formal response from the government to the report handed down earlier this year.

New restrictions to protect fish stocks

The bloom's effect on fish stocks has prompted an intensification of restrictions on certain catches and Mr Malinauskas said authorities remained "very concerned" about squid.

"There is very little sign of … calamari in either the Gulf of St Vincent or the Spencer Gulf," he said.

"There have already been significant calamari closures but now they are being extended across both gulfs for recreational and commercial."

Dead fish at Corny Point on the south-west Yorke Peninsula in January. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

RecFish SA executive director Asher Dezsery backed that move.

"There are no catches of calamari currently occurring, but there are some eggs being observed," he said.

"We all have to come together as a community and make sure that we support these species as they recover, and I don't think we will hear many arguments over making sure that these fish bounce back as fast as possible."

Several Gulf St Vincent fishers have previously urged for an indefinite closure of that fishery, with one warning that it "would be horrendous to reopen" before stocks had rejuvenated.

"All key species in Gulf St Vincent are near non-existent levels," Ardrossan calamari fisher, Michael Pennington, told the ABC before Easter.

RecFish SA executive director Asher Dezsery backed a move to extend restrictions on calamari fishing. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Port Lincoln fisher Jarrod Day today welcomed the new restrictions, and said they "certainly will help".

"It's sort of hard to swallow, but the fact is the species needs to be looked after, and looked after sooner rather than later," he said.

Mr Day said he had recently been out fishing, and that catches tended to be around 10 kilograms — significantly less than the "at least 50 kilos" that he would expect "on an average day".

Jarrod Day is a commercial fisher operating out of Port Lincoln. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Duncan Bailey)

"Small quantities are getting caught at the moment — we are still catching, but very, very small amounts. Not really what I'd call large commercial quantities.

"The price has been quite good for calamari because of the lack of supply, but that doesn't necessarily make up for the lack of fish."

Scientists may have found SA algal bloom brevetoxin source Scientists believe they have identified the species responsible for the toxins in South Australia's marine algal bloom that has killed millions of aquatic animals.

Professor Steer defended the time it had taken to impose the additional restrictions on calamari catches.

"[Calamari] grow really quickly," he said.

"They spawn all year round, so you have a continual conveyer belt of calamari spawning throughout a health ecosystem."

But new restrictions will also come into effect for other species including garfish, with a "recreational and charter boat closure" in Gulf St Vincent.

"Our iconic King George whiting — the premium South Australian fish — has also indicated some levels of decline, and we are re-implementing a … spawning closure in the southern area around Yorke Peninsula," Professor Steer said.

"Down in the deeper waters of the southern gulfs, that's where the large, mature individuals will spawn, and are effectively the engine room of replenishment for those stocks."

Heartbreak of toxic algal bloom outbreak A mysterious, brown foam appeared on a beach an hour south of Adelaide. It was just the beginning of a toxic algal bloom that has now grown to thousands of square kilometres in size, killing precious sea life in its wake. Experts say it could be a sign of things to come.

That closure will apply until the end of July, Professor Steer said.

But the government said blue swimmer crab numbers in Gulf St Vincent were sufficiently abundant to allow for a removal of restrictions.

"Crabbing — it's back on with a gusto, and likewise for commercial crabbers they can go about their business as per usual," Mr Malinauskas said.

"Blue swimmer crab numbers are performing extremely well — extremely well — to the extent that we're now in a position where we can completely reopen that fishery, both for commercially and recreationally, with usual bag limits now being restored."

World.title: Pogačar looks unbeatable, but Seixas could be France's next new hope
World.content:
Tadej Pogačar has long looked unstoppable in cycling's biggest races.

The Slovenian two-time world champion continued in that vein on Sunday, winning a third monument victory of the year at the 259.5 kilometre-long Liège-Bastogne-Liège.

It was his third La Doyenne title in a row and fourth overall in a career that has seen him already claim 13 monuments — cycling's five major one-day races: Milan-San Remo, Ronde van Vlaanderen, Paris-Roubaix, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and Giro di Lombardia.

However, this time it was not quite so easy, as 19-year-old French star Paul Seixas delivered an ominous reminder of his rising star with a powerful performance to take second place on debut.

No French rider has won the men's Liège-Bastogne-Liège title since five-times Tour de France winner Bernard Hinault did so in 1980 — a victory in the midst of the last great era for French men's road cycling.

The cupboard has been pretty bare in recent years in terms of a rider capable of regularly challenging the world's best.

But, in Seixas, France has a(nother) new hope to pin its dreams on.

Paul Seixas won the 90th edition of La Flèche Wallonne with a sizzling attack up the Mur de Huy. (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

Winner of three stages and the overall classification at last week's Itzulia Basque Country and the La Flèche Wallonne one-day classic on Wednesday, Seixas came into the fourth monument of the year in fine form and high on confidence.

Pogačar launched his now-standard assault on the brutal Côte de la Redoute climb 35km from the finish, dropping the rest of the field with brutal efficiency.

However, alongside him was the teen Frenchman from the Decathlon CMA CGM team.

"I went really deep up La Redoute, and I could see Paul was struggling, but then he came near me across the summit," Pogačar said at the finish, expressing his admiration.

Very few riders have the capability to ride with Pogačar when he launches his blistering attacks; too many have been burned by flying so close to the sun.

But Seixas not only soared along with the Slovenian superstar, but pulled his way to help the pair extend the gap.

Where far too many others have seen the wax melting from their wings, Seixas's were barely clipped.

That is, until Pogačar sent the pace into the stratosphere to leave Seixas faltering on the final ascent up the Côte de la Roche-aux-Faucons with less than 14km left in the race, condemning the Frenchman to a lonely ride home for second, 45 seconds behind.

"He pulled quite strong all the way [to the Côte de la Roche-aux-Faucons] and because of this we were able to open a big gap," Pogačar said.

"In the back of my mind, I was getting ready to go head-to-head on a sprint with him … luckily I managed to drop him."

Expectation already reaching fever pitch of Tour de France assault

Could we see a podium made up of Paul Seixas (left), Tadej Pogačar (centre) and Remco Evenepoel (right) at the Tour de France? (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

With the spring classics campaign largely done and dusted, attention is now turning to the year's grand tours.

The Giro d'Italia gets underway in May, but Pogačar will be absent from the quest for the maglia rosa, instead once more looking to France and a fifth victory in La Grande Boucle.

There is an expectation that Seixas will join him.

There is also a suspicion that Seixas may even challenge him.

"I am impressed and amazed by how good Paul is — chapeau to him," Pogačar said.

"I have nothing but praise for the kid — for his incredible results at the start of this season, and for how mature he is.

"I don't think there are many riders stronger than him right now.

"Having him at such a good level, being just 19 years old, is a source of motivation for everybody to keep trying to improve, he is just 19yo and the best age for us riders usually is 26 or 28.

"We have to keep working hard if we want to keep fighting for victories, before he destroys everybody.

Tadej Pogačar has won four Liège–Bastogne–Liège races. (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

"I definitely know that every year it will become harder and harder for me to win. I've been doing this for a while now, and I'm not getting any younger. It's a matter of time before I decline."

Two-time Liège-Bastogne-Liège winner Remco Evenepoel, who is also expected to challenge for the Tour de France title in July and August, finished in third place in Liège.

He is under no illusions that Seixas will be a significant challenger in France later this year, despite his inexperience.

"It seems Paul was more than ready for a 6-hour race," Evenepoel said of the question marks that had been raised over Seixas's endurance.

"It was not surprising that he was able to follow Tadej up La Redoute, because we know his results and his performances from the previous months.

"He showed again today that he already is one of the best climbers in the world, and on top of this, has a great punch in him.

"The whole world can only say 'chapeau' to him. It's great that he can already fight for the win in big races like Liège-Bastogne-Liège."

Pressure to suffocate Paul? Not likely

Is this a race situation we will see at the 2026 Tour de France? (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

The pressure on any pretender to the throne upon which France's fanatical cycling supporters place their champions is unparalleled.

It's a lot for any rider to handle, let alone one so young.

French monument winners this century Thibaut Pinot, Arnaud Démare and Julian Alaphilippe have all at one stage carried the burden of expectation upon their shoulders and found that carrying that across the passes of the Alps and Pyrenees is too much of a load to bear.

The expectation in the French press is already in danger of being suffocating — there has even been an unsubstantiated rumour that President of the Republic Emmanuel Macron intervened to keep Siexas at his French team Decathlon, rather than fall into another team's hands, such would be the glory to France if he were to win Le Tour with a French team.

But Seixas has stayed calm.

"You have to take things one step at a time, without rushing," he said.

"At Strade Bianche [where Siexas finished a distant second behind Pogačar], I couldn't follow his first attack; today I managed to do it, so I'm quite happy with my performance.

Seixas has proven he can do it in the Ardennes, what about across three weeks of France's most varied landscapes? (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

"I always race to win, but we know that Pogačar has been utterly dominant these last few years, so just being able to follow him is already something.

"Just keeping up with Pogačar is extremely difficult. He's one of the greatest riders of all time, so being able to hang on to him, to fight with him all the way to Roche-aux-Faucons.

"There's still work to be done, and that's normal; we mustn't rush things, but be satisfied with what we got today."

Seixas acknowledged that he was "completely exhausted" by the time the race got to La Redoute, describing the pace as "insane" and that he was already in "uncharted territory" given the superior length of monuments compared to most other one-day races.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

However, he said that he had made a "step forward" with his endurance" and his attributes suited repeat efforts.

"How hard the race was almost works to my advantage because I can repeat efforts and recover quite well from them, as we saw at the Tour of the Basque Country," he said.

"It's very satisfying for the future."

That last sentence is a phrase likely to be gobbled up by the French press as they start their campaign for him to start the Tour de France for the first time in his fledgling career later this year.

But Seixas knows that he needs to be patient.

"My next ambition will be to win a Monument," Seixas said.

"There are no certainties in life regarding the future: until you've done it, you haven't done it. I'm just going to work towards it."

World.title: Indigenous veteran booed at Anzac Day service 'mortified' by heckling
World.content:
The Whadjuk Noongar elder who was booed while giving a Welcome to Country at Perth's Anzac Day dawn service says she was "mortified" but will not back down.

Army veteran and community leader Di Ryder had just started her speech on Saturday morning, saying "welcome to Noongar country", when some in the crowd began to boo.

The interjections became louder when she continued by outlining her military service, at which point Ms Ryder paused, repeated herself, and continued with her speech.

Loading...

"It was distracting, I've got to be honest, but then I thought 'I'm here for a reason'," she told 102.5 ABC Radio.

"The reason was to welcome people to Noongar Boodja and that's what I stood firm with.

"I had a right to be standing up there as a veteran and also a Noongar elder, and for me that was the thing, I should have been able to be there without being booed.

"I am mortified that it happened on Anzac Day."

Ms Ryder's address was also interrupted a second time when she paid respect to "elders past and present" and acknowledged "our young people who will take our Noongar culture into the future".

Perth ANZAC Day hecklers condemned as 'disgusting, cretins' Leaders have condemned "cretins" who interjected and booed at Perth and Western Australian Anzac Day ceremonies, with the premier labelling their actions "disgusting and disrespectful".

Leaders were quick to condemn the booing, with RSL WA chief executive Stephen Barton telling the crowd "we will not be bullied" and Premier Roger Cook labelling the booing "disgusting and disrespectful".

Police issued five people with move-on notices after the heckling, in addition to five that were handed out before the service began.

"I can't put into words how I felt that they would use that day to platform something like the Welcome to Country," Ms Ryder said.

Time to 'make a stand'

The community leader said she had expected to be booed after a similar incident last year, but that it did little to soften the blow.

"As an Aboriginal person, you just accept that this is the way things will go until we make a stand, like the RSL did on Saturday," Ms Ryder said.

She stood by Welcome to Country addresses as an important opportunity to acknowledge all Indigenous veterans who served in conflicts as far back as the Boer War, which Australia was involved in between 1899 and 1902.

Di Ryder with WA Governor Chris Dawson after she delivered her Welcome to Country address. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"There were many that served in World War I, World War II, but also the Korean War, the Vietnam War and all wars, conflicts and peacekeeping and even in time of peace," she said.

"So we have been there right from the Boer War to the present, and we do have a right to be acknowledged as well."

RSL issues appeal

RSL national president Peter Tinley said the behaviour was "disgusting" and showed "disrespect".

"I want to apologise as national president of the RSL to Di Ryder and every other Indigenous person that was basically assaulted for being Australian and having been proud of their heritage on a day when we should be inclusive of everybody's heritage, particularly First Nations people," he told 102.5 ABC Radio.

Peter Tinley, the RSL's national president, called out the racism. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Mr Tinley said the RSL would be speaking to the Australian Federal Police about what measures to put in place at future events.

But he said it was "the majority" that would stop similar heckling in the future, urging people: "If you see racism around, you've got to fight it where you find it."

"And if somebody next to you is booing and carrying on, you get the police's attention and you call them out," Mr Tinley said.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor yesterday condemned the booing but said Welcome to Country ceremonies were overused, arguing that "devalued" them.

Police were on hand at Kings Park in Perth for the dawn service on Saturday. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

Ms Ryder agreed they could be overused, but said they were appropriate at dawn services.

"This is a ceremony where we're honouring where we're living or where we're standing on Noongar country," she said.

"But it's also about the respect shown for those Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people that did serve."

Mr Tinley said there was a place for Welcome to Country addresses at dawn services "if the community wants it", but that the decision was left to individual RSL sub-branches and organising groups.

Premier rejects 'hatred'

WA Premier Roger Cook described the booing as the orchestrated actions of extremists who must be stopped from bringing hatred and division into the community.

Roger Cook says Welcome to Country addresses should be observed and respected. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"What this does show is there are extremist elements out there that are seeking to disrupt the consensus and the unity of our community," he said.

"We can't let them divide. We can't let them sow the hatred in our community that they seek."

Anzac Day booing a legacy of failed Voice referendum Jeers could be heard for more than a minute as Uncle Ray Minniecon spoke at Saturday's Anzac service in Sydney — with similar scenes playing out during the Welcome to Country in Melbourne and Perth.

Asked about the sentiment that Welcome to Country ceremonies could be overused, Mr Cook said he always observed the addresses.

"Because that is what our First Nations people say is appropriate, given the oldest traditions and culture that sits in this land.

"If one of theirs makes an observation about that, that's up to them. But I just do what's respectful."

World.title: PNG PM says Luai's visit 'sends a message' ahead of Chiefs' NRL entry
World.content:
Papua New Guinea's prime minister has declared that Jarome Luai's visit to Port Moresby "sends a message" the nation's NRL team is ready to hit the ground running.

The Wests Tigers playmaker was pictured in the PNG capital on Sunday where he met with PNG Chiefs officials and watched a game of the domestic national competition.

"To be the first high-profile player to come and show interest in our team is something we deeply appreciate," PNG Prime Minister James Marape told local media.

"It sends a message that Papua New Guinea is ready, rugby league is strong here, and our future in the NRL is bright."

James Marape says Luai's trip to the country shows it is ready to embrace the NRL. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Luai is signed to the Tigers until the end of 2029 but his deal, believed to be worth $1.2 million a season, has exit clauses that allow him to depart early.

The four-time premiership winner has until Thursday to indicate to the Tigers if he will remain with the club in 2027.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

That appears a formality given the Tigers' 5-2 start this season but where it gets interesting is when the PNG Chiefs enter the NRL in 2028.

Luai could massively increase his pay packet with the tax-free status afforded to NRL players as well as boost his earnings through third-party arrangements in a rugby league-obsessed country such as PNG.

"At this stage, there is nothing formal or concrete," Mr Marape said.

"Jarome remains contracted to the Wests Tigers, and we fully respect his current obligations.

"We are a nation that honours due process, and we respect clubs, contracts, and the professionalism of the game."

Mr Marape also thanked Tigers coach Benji Marshall for allowing Luai to make the flying visit to Port Moresby.

The Chiefs, who will be led by Hull KR coach Willie Peters, have yet to sign a player for their maiden season but have been linked to Sydney Roosters and NSW State of Origin utility Connor Watson.

World.title: 'We live up here to escape': Residents unhappy with sand dredging proposal
World.content:
A proposal to dredge 70 million cubic metres of sand from northern Western Australia for export to Asia has faced opposition from local community members.

Boskalis Australia is looking to develop a marine sand sourcing operation in Cambridge Gulf on the north coast of Western Australia's Kimberley region, about 3,000 kilometres from Perth.

The project received conditional approval from the WA Environmental Protection Authority late last year.

The proposed operational area is located in the central part of the main body of Cambridge Gulf, and covers an area of about 100 square kilometres. (Supplied: Boskalis Australia Pty Ltd)

As part of Boskalis's "ongoing consultation process", the Netherlands-based maritime services company held public meetings in Kununurra and Wyndham this month.

The towns are the closest to the proposed project site.

Kununurra-raised fisher Brad Pasfield attended both meetings and said the atmosphere was charged.

"I think people are just really passionate, and people don't care about what money is involved; people care about the broader picture," he said.

"It's what's going to happen in the future … the potential damages on the environment.

" It's just too close to home. We live up here to escape things like this. "

Operational presence in Cambridge Gulf would be up to two days a fortnight. (Supplied: Boskalis Australia Pty Ltd)

Mr Pasfield said he was disappointed by Boskalis's efforts to engage with the community.

"I think people feel very blindsided," he said.

"Lack of consultation is massive. People need to be kept informed."

The Kununurra resident previously operated a fishing charter business that primarily fished the Cambridge Gulf.

He said he had planned to recommence operations in the near future, but the project — if it went ahead — would create "a few more hurdles".

"My biggest concern is the ecosystem and keeping that intact," he said.

"Which goes down to the smaller fish and insects and small creatures that live under the water and under the soil."

Feedback is a 'lesson learned'

Boskalis Australia's general manager Alwin van den Bosch said the proposed operation would have no significant environmental impact, but acknowledged the company had not clearly communicated its plans to the public.

"We think we have a very solid case for undertaking this work in a safe, social and environmentally friendly manner, but I think the perception among the public was clear that communication hasn't been there," he said.

"They have not been aware of all that work which we have been doing."

Alwin van den Bosch says the project would have no significant environmental impact. (ABC Kimberley: Jess Baker)

Mr van den Bosch said a "concerted stakeholder consultation effort" began in 2022 and was still ongoing.

He said the company accepted some community members felt public meetings should have happened earlier.

"That is a lesson learned," he said.

The proposed operation is vessel-based and would not involve the construction and operation of any marine or shore-based infrastructure.

There would be a "sand production vessel" operating in Cambridge Gulf for a total of 52 days a year, self-loading sand for one or two days a fortnight.

The vessel would remove a layer of about 40 centimetres of sand from the seabed during a loading cycle, then sail to Asia, returning to the gulf two weeks later to repeat the process.

Sand will 'naturally replenish'

Mr van den Bosch said up to 70 million cubic metres of sand would be removed and exported over 15 years, after which time the seabed within the 100-square-kilometre proposed operational area would be about 1 metre lower.

"There is way more sand present in that area than we are planning to extract," he said.

"And that is without taking into consideration the natural replenishment of that area because … there is a natural inflow of sand from all the tributaries, which replenish the sand which we take away."

Conceptual depiction of a sand production vessel, which would self-load sand in the Cambridge Gulf. (Supplied: Boskalis Australia Pty Ltd)

Mr van den Bosch said 10 to 15 million cubic metres of sand flowed back into the system each year — a factor that, combined with the site's barrenness and proximity to Asia, made it suitable for the project.

"We've looked at the environmental impact which we could cause to a certain area, the wildlife, which is present in the area, the marine fauna," he said.

"This area we have selected is devoid of that.

"There is very little marine wildlife, very little marine flora, simply because of the characteristics of the area: there's an enormous tidal range, there is a lot of natural movement of the sand dunes."

Appeals being assessed

The WA Environmental Protection Authority released its report for the sand proposal in November and recommended it be implemented, subject to conditions.

Following an appeal period that closed in December, the Office of the Appeals Convenor must assess the appeals received and then make recommendations to the WA environment minister, who will make a final decision.

A state government spokesperson said the appeals convenor would likely submit her recommendations this year.

World.title: Promise of $1b to fix Victorian roads in upcoming budget
World.content:
The Victorian government has pledged more than $1 billion to fix roads and clean up graffiti along thoroughfares across the state.

The $1.04 billion investment in the upcoming budget, which the government is calling a record for the state, will repair arterial roads, bridges and roadside signs.

Minister for Roads Ros Spence said it represented "record investment" in the state's roads.

"Importantly, 70 per cent of this funding is going to regional Victoria where we know that safe and reliable roads are absolutely critical," she said.

" The investment will fix around 200,000 potholes and remove around 200,000 graffiti tags. "

Funding will also go towards mowing grass and spraying weeds along roadsides, as well as include a $36.9 million package to clean up graffiti and rubbish along major freeways such as the Monash, Calder and Hume.

"This funding will enable us to prioritise Melbourne's 10 busiest freeways and really focus in on those areas of priority for the Victorian community," Premier Jacinta Allan said.

Millions will be invested into cleaning graffiti near major highways around the state. (Instagram)

Frustration remains high among some Victorian motorists about poor quality roads across the state.

Hundreds of Victorians lodge claims each year for damage to their vehicles as a result of poor roads, with only about one per cent approved for compensation.

Ms Allan said most of the money would be spent outside of Melbourne.

"As a result of the extreme heavy weather and flooding events that occurred across 2022, 2023 and 2024, that has created some real challenges on our road network," she said.

"There are parts of regional Victoria that were hit multiple times, that's why you've got to keep up the effort."

A 2025 report revealed that rural and regional areas host the most dangerous roads in Victoria, with some local councils saying they are caught in an arm wrestle with the state government for funding to repair them.

'No real change', says opposition

The quality of Victoria's roads has been used as a major campaign target for the opposition ahead of both the state election and the upcoming Nepean by-election.

Shadow Roads Minister Danny O'Brien said the increase in funding announced by the government represented only a "slight increase" which when factoring in inflation, would represent "no real change".

"This is the annual maintenance funding for our roads that comes out every year," he said.

" Frankly its not enough because the government has neglected our roads for over a decade. "

A pothole more than 1.5 metres long in north-east Victoria. (Supplied: Member for Benambra)

The funding represents a $64 million, or just over 6.5 per cent, increase on the previous year's allocation.

Ms Spence rejected the opposition's criticism and maintained it was additional funding.

"We know that there's more work to be done and that's why this funding is really important," she said.

"This will go to the rebuild, repair and resurface of roads right across Victoria."

The Liberal Party's candidate for the Nepean by-election, Anthony Marsh, performed unauthorised roadworks as part of a campaign stunt with Opposition Leader Jess Wilson earlier this month.

The social media stunt, which featured Mr Marsh and Ms Wilson filling in potholes in the suburb of Dromana, is now the subject of a complaint to the state's Department of Transport and Planning.

World.title: Who's who in Tasmania's upper house elections this weekend
World.content:
Tens of thousands of Tasmanians will be voting in this weekend's upper house elections — with two seats up for grabs.

In the state's south, Huon's independent incumbent, Dean Harriss, will be hoping to hold onto the seat, while in the seat of Rosevears in the state's north Liberal Education Minister Jo Palmer will be trying to fight off challengers.

The outcome of both elections may help shape whether greyhound racing will be banned in the state, with the government delaying an upper house vote on the issue until later in May in the hope of winning over enough independents.

Any changes to the makeup of the chamber after Saturday's elections could make it easier or harder for the government to get its legislation through the parliament. ( )

The Legislative Council or upper house is known as the house of review because its primary job is to scrutinise bills passed by the lower house.

It is currently dominated by independents who hold eight of the 15 seats.

The government and Labor each hold three, and the Greens one.

Each upper house member is elected for a six-year term, and elections are held on a rotating basis, offering more stability than the lower house, which has had three elections in the past six years.

Not sure who to vote for? These are the candidates standing for election:

Huon

Dean Harriss (Incumbent, independent) Dean Harriss is recontesting the seat of Huon. ( ) Independent Dean Harriss believes his background in construction has helped him in politics. "That practical 'can do, get results' has been good for me, but [politics] has been challenging as well," he said. Mr Harriss, whose father Paul served as a Legislative Councillor for 18 years, is a big believer in having independents in the Upper House. "We're there to provide the checks and balances on legislation and I strongly believe that can only be done through independents," he said. "Being able to, one, not be told what to do by party-aligned members and party leaders, but also being able to drill down into the details, and understand people's concerns and vote accordingly on that." He says the main issue for people in Huon is the cost of living — from health to housing, groceries and rates. While Mr Harriss thinks the government has handled the whole greyhound situation "pretty badly" he is willing to support the bill to ban the sport if it improves the industry compensation package. "Social license is important as well, and some of that has been lost in the greyhound industry," he said. "But … it's very important that people within the industry have the option to exit the industry with dignity." Asked what his values are, Mr Harris says he's "community focused". "Huon's where I've grown up, it's where we're raising our four kids and I think to give back to that is pretty important," he said. Clare Glade-Wright (Independent) Clare Glade-Wright is running as in independent for the seat of Huon. ( ) Deputy Mayor of Kingborough Clare Glade-Wright has a strong grassroots campaign behind her with nearly 140 volunteers. The independent candidate says she has two things she really wants to champion if she wins a seat in the Legislative Council — a program to clean up waterways in the Huon and Channel, and a rule change for tiny homes. "Kingborough Council and Huon Valley Council … want to approve tiny houses, but the way the rules are set up, there's no easy pathway for compliance," she says. Ms Glade-Wright says as deputy mayor she is known for "being visible and accessible and engaging" and that's something she would bring to parliament. "It is apparent that the community down here in Huon are actually really frustrated with their incumbent, with the level of representation that they are receiving," she said. "So I think I step really nicely into that need." And she's adamant the upper house needs to have independents for "true scrutiny". "If we have party politicians in the upper house, it's a completely wasted seat," she said. "They don't have to do any work. All they have to do is endorse what was said by their party members down below." On the issue of greyhound racing, Ms Glade-Wright says she would vote to end the industry. Michael Rowan (Independent) Michael Rowan is contesting Huon as an independent. ( ) A professor of philosophy who moved to Tasmania almost two decades ago, Michael Rowan describes himself as a "reluctant candidate". He's spent most of his life out of politics, but he's concerned about the quality of the government in Tasmania and around the world. "Right now we are not on a course to leave our children and grandchildren a world as safe, prosperous and beautiful as the world in which we grew up," he said. "I think I have an obligation to do all that I can to make sure that that happens." Mr Rowan has three main issues he wants to address if he wins a seat in the Legislative Council: the budget, education and the environment. "I think Tasmania needs to completely rewrite its Environment Act using the best examples in the world, and I think that's currently Estonia," he says. "On education, we have an appalling record of children completing year 12, although lower down, like the NAPLAN results at year 3 are outstanding. "We need to improve the budget in Tasmania by $300 million a year for five years in a row before we can start paying back our debt." On greyhound racing, Mr Rowan says he's predisposed against it but he would wait to hear the debate. Paul Gibson (Green) Paul Gibson is running for the Greens in Huon. ( ) Paul Gibson has been representing his community on the Huon Valley Council for the past eight years, but he's ready to take it one step further. "I really am a firm believer that it's government's role to look after communities and to work for them," he said. Mr Gibson believes the reason people might be tempted to vote independent is because they want to avoid the Labor and Liberal parties, but he argues "the Greens are the true opposition". "The thing with the Greens is you know what you're getting," he says. "You know that we'll stick to it. We're not going to be picked off like independents were for the stadium debate." Like the other candidates, he says the main issue most people are bringing up is cost of living. "Housing, young people just can't get housing, they can't live in the towns down here because it's all just too expensive," he said. Asked what he would bring compared with the other candidates, Mr Gibson says he has a "history of standing up for good governance". "I'm a very strong community supporter, I'm very active volunteer in my community in suicide prevention," he said. "I believe the government should be listening to and responding to and working for communities and unfortunately the two major parties work for big business rather than communities." The Greens will support the greyhound racing ban. Tyler Petersen (Independent) Tyler Petersen is an independent candidate for Huon. ( ) Tyler Petersen describes himself as "the true independent" because he's "not softly backed by a political party or an interest group". "I think for myself, and I don't think I could toe a party line," he says. " I want to be able to vote with my conscience, 100 per cent. " As a renter with a young family, Mr Petersen says he's passionate about cost of living. "It's not a policy paper for me or a talking point; it's a lived reality," he says. Mr Petersen says he'd "like to make noise and be a voice for regular people". "As ideas are coming up from the lower house, if they're foolish, I can advocate for normal people, for regular people who are feeling the pension, they're going to the bowser and trying to decide if they're going to fill up the car or if they're going to buy groceries, are they going to pay the power bill in instalments or can they pay it up-front? "If those policies aren't right when they're coming out of the lower house, I'll send it back." Mr Petersen says he'll vote to end greyhound racing. Abby McKibben (Labor) Abby McKibbon is Labor's candidate for the seat of Huon. ( ) Abby McKibben has lived in the Huon Valley for almost 25 years. "Professionally, I've got a really good breadth of experience in industries that are really relevant to the Huon — aquaculture, agriculture, tourism, local business and now in local government," she says. "I think I could be really effective for the people of Huon and a really positive, constructive voice for them." Ms McKibben says in her time in Huon she's watched many local members come and go. "Often we don't hear or see them once they've gotten the nod," she says. "The Legislative Council only sits for about 14 weeks of the year so that leaves 38 weeks for us to have someone out in the community being a really active voice and championing not just local issues but local opportunities that we see here in the Huon," she says. Ms McKibben says while having some independent representation in parliament is important, she believes being in a party will allow her to achieve much more. "I chose deliberately to stand with Labor as a party member so that I can champion issues and opportunities through the party channels — both state and federally — and get things actually achieved here for the people of the Huon," she says. Ms McKibben wants to champion childcare services, healthcare and cost of living. She says she supports Labor's decision to oppose the phase out of greyhound racing.

Rosevears

World.title: 'Superhero' politician shielded Kerry Kennedy at correspondents' dinner
World.content:
Lawyer and human rights activist Kerry Kennedy has praised a "superhero" member of Congress for shielding her when an active shooter attempted to storm the annual White House Correspondents' Association dinner in Washington, DC.

Gunshots rang out inside the Washington Hilton at about 8:35pm, local time, prompting hundreds of journalists, photographers and dignitaries in the subterranean ballroom to take cover beneath tables and chairs.

Trump dinner shooting live updates: For the latest news on the White House Correspondents' Association dinner shooting, read our blog.

Ms Kennedy said she was mid-conversation with Jamie Raskin, a Democratic representative for Maryland, when the room fell into disarray.

"Suddenly, people started yelling, 'Get down, get down,'" she told MS NOW on Sunday.

"So I immediately laid down and my head was on the lap of a Boston Globe journalist and my knees were on a United States senator, and then Jamie just used his whole body to shield me like the hero that he is and he kept whispering, 'You're OK, you're OK, you're OK.'"

Moments later, Secret Service agents spilled into the room and began evacuating cabinet members.

"You could see the terror on the eyes of the people they were pulling out of the room," Ms Kennedy said.

Robert F Kennedy Jr and his wife, Cheryl Hines, were evacuated from the room by security officials. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

Among them was Ms Kennedy's brother, Secretary of Health Robert F Kennedy Jr, though she did not see him or his wife, Cheryl Hines, get whisked away by agents.

Kerry and Robert's father, Robert F Kennedy, was assassinated in 1968 at the Ambassador Hotel in California while campaigning for the Democratic Party's presidential nomination.

ABC reporter at Trump dinner when shots rang out ABC Americas editor was inside the ballroom when a shooting suspect was stopped by the Secret Service.

Their uncle, John F Kennedy Jr, had been assassinated five years earlier in Texas.

"I was just thinking so much about my dad, who was killed by a shooter in a situation like that; about my incredibly mighty mother, who was … pregnant at the time with her 11th child."

Ms Kennedy estimated the chaos lasted about five minutes before people rose to their feet again.

"During those minutes, I was so scared. It was like my body could not move — I had no control of my body," she said.

"It was just this kind of whimpering coming out of my mouth, which I had no control of."

She said she was grateful for Mr Raskin and for the Secret Service agents who responded to the incident.

"… [He] is such a superhero, just putting his life on the line to protect me," she said.

Jamie Raskin outside the Washington Hilton after the shooting. (AFP: Alex Wroblewski)

The alleged suspect, who has been identified by several US outlets as 31-year-old teacher and engineer Cole Tomas Allen, was armed with a shotgun, a handgun and multiple knives, according to police.

Mr Raskin told CNN the "first thing" Ms Kennedy said after the chaos subsided was: "This is happening in schools across the country, and kids have no resources to process their trauma."

"She was talking about gun violence and thinking about other people. She's a great human rights activist," he said.

"And nobody wants to be in a situation like that, but I was glad to have been with her."

Kerry Kennedy has served as president of the Robert F Kennedy Human Rights organisation since 1981. (AFP: Astrid Stawiarz/Getty Images for RFK Ripple Of Hope)

Ms Kennedy used her appearance on MS NOW to call for stronger gun control laws.

"Just think about all these children, kindergarteners, who are experiencing the same thing in their schools in our country," she said.

"Why? There's no reason for this, and that's something that doesn't happen in other countries — it just doesn't happen. It's all about access to guns.

"I mean, we have to stop this insanity in our country with allowing anybody and everybody to buy guns and make it so easy for them to buy guns.

"You know, there are more gun dealers than there are McDonald's in our country. We've got to stop this."

A 2023 report by Everytown for Gun Safety found the US had nearly 78,000 licensed gun dealers — more than the number of McDonald's, Burger King, Subway and Wendy's locations combined.

Citing law enforcement documents and a senior official, NBC News reported the suspected gunman, Mr Allen, bought his guns legally.

World.title: Viking advances Nevada tungsten play as prices hit record highs
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Viking advances Nevada tungsten play as prices hit record highs Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS James Pearson April 27, 2026 — 1:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Viking Mines appears to have wasted little time advancing its Linka tungsten project in Nevada, moving into early-stage processing design work using a nifty modular plant design as it pushes the critical minerals play towards a genuine development story. Fresh from earlier metallurgical work that delivered a saleable concentrate grading an impressive 63.6 per cent tungsten trioxide, the company says consultant Mineral Technologies has now finalised a preliminary process flow diagram for the project. Old workings at Viking Mines’ Linka tungsten project in Nevada. The milestone marks a meaningful moment for Viking. A metallurgical win in the lab is now starting to translate into the practical nuts and bolts of mine development, including equipment sizing, indicative capital and operating costs and construction planning. As part of the study, the company says it has adopted a notional processing rate of 43 tonnes per hour, emphasising this is not a production forecast, rather a planning assumption to help shape equipment needs and preliminary project economics.



‘Defining conceptual processing steps for Linka is a significant step.’ Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock Notably, the proposed plant design has been built with flexibility at its core. Management believes a flowsheet using a modular approach could allow future additions, such as Wet High-Intensity Magnetic Separation (WHIMS) or a Falcon concentrator, if subsequent test work points to stronger recoveries. Optionality is often valuable in mining, particularly for specialty metals such as tungsten, where recoveries and concentrate can materially impact project economics. Mineral Technologies has now begun specification and sizing work on mechanical equipment, which is expected to feed into early cost estimates. At the same time, Viking says it’s continuing test work on rock breakage and energy usage, supported by newly collected metallurgical samples. The results are expected to provide early guidance on power demand, water and reagent requirements.



Additionally, the company says it’s assessing whether certain plant modules, including the crushing circuit, should be purchased outright or leased to reduce upfront capital costs and shorten development lead times. The approach suggests a capital-light strategy, favouring disciplined, staged project development over bigger, funding-heavy build plans. Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock said: “Mineral Technologies has designed a process flow that is both robust and flexible, allowing us to maintain a capital-efficient pathway to potential future development while keeping the ability to add additional recovery stages later.” On the exploration front, Viking has signalled it expects to begin drilling later in the June quarter, ramping up a phase-two field program featuring geological mapping and follow-up of targets generated from gravity and magnetic geophysics, alongside historical trench results. The company is also finalising a 3D geological model to sharpen drill targeting and potentially underpin a future JORC exploration target. The company’s program appears well timed, with the global tungsten market continuing to grapple with a severe supply squeeze. Prices for ammonium paratungstate recently climbed to record highs of US$318.50 (A$448.50) per metric tonne unit, with one MTU equal to 10 kilograms of material.



The sharp run-up in prices has thrust Viking’s Nevada assets into sharper focus as Western supply chains hunt for secure, reliable tungsten sources. In a bid to fast-track early cash flow and capitalise on record prices, the company has started quantifying historical above-ground stockpiles and material within a sizeable tailings dam. The stockpiles are now being tested to confirm the high-grade potential of this low-cost feed source, building on earlier due diligence samples collected late last year that returned 0.8 per cent tungsten trioxide. In parallel with the stockpile assessment, Viking has launched a grid-sampling program across the project’s tailings dam to estimate its volume, tonnage and potential economic value as an additional feed source for immediate processing or toll treatment. With tungsten increasingly recognised as a strategic metal critical to defence, industrial tooling and high-performance alloys, Linka is shaping as a timely project in a prime jurisdiction.



If maiden drilling delivers and early economics stack up, Viking’s Linka tungsten project in Nevada could soon evolve into a serious new tungsten contender. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Viking advances Nevada tungsten play as prices hit record highs
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Viking advances Nevada tungsten play as prices hit record highs Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS James Pearson April 27, 2026 — 1:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Viking Mines appears to have wasted little time advancing its Linka tungsten project in Nevada, moving into early-stage processing design work using a nifty modular plant design as it pushes the critical minerals play towards a genuine development story. Fresh from earlier metallurgical work that delivered a saleable concentrate grading an impressive 63.6 per cent tungsten trioxide, the company says consultant Mineral Technologies has now finalised a preliminary process flow diagram for the project. Old workings at Viking Mines’ Linka tungsten project in Nevada. The milestone marks a meaningful moment for Viking. A metallurgical win in the lab is now starting to translate into the practical nuts and bolts of mine development, including equipment sizing, indicative capital and operating costs and construction planning. As part of the study, the company says it has adopted a notional processing rate of 43 tonnes per hour, emphasising this is not a production forecast, rather a planning assumption to help shape equipment needs and preliminary project economics.



‘Defining conceptual processing steps for Linka is a significant step.’ Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock Notably, the proposed plant design has been built with flexibility at its core. Management believes a flowsheet using a modular approach could allow future additions, such as Wet High-Intensity Magnetic Separation (WHIMS) or a Falcon concentrator, if subsequent test work points to stronger recoveries. Optionality is often valuable in mining, particularly for specialty metals such as tungsten, where recoveries and concentrate can materially impact project economics. Mineral Technologies has now begun specification and sizing work on mechanical equipment, which is expected to feed into early cost estimates. At the same time, Viking says it’s continuing test work on rock breakage and energy usage, supported by newly collected metallurgical samples. The results are expected to provide early guidance on power demand, water and reagent requirements.



Additionally, the company says it’s assessing whether certain plant modules, including the crushing circuit, should be purchased outright or leased to reduce upfront capital costs and shorten development lead times. The approach suggests a capital-light strategy, favouring disciplined, staged project development over bigger, funding-heavy build plans. Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock said: “Mineral Technologies has designed a process flow that is both robust and flexible, allowing us to maintain a capital-efficient pathway to potential future development while keeping the ability to add additional recovery stages later.” On the exploration front, Viking has signalled it expects to begin drilling later in the June quarter, ramping up a phase-two field program featuring geological mapping and follow-up of targets generated from gravity and magnetic geophysics, alongside historical trench results. The company is also finalising a 3D geological model to sharpen drill targeting and potentially underpin a future JORC exploration target. The company’s program appears well timed, with the global tungsten market continuing to grapple with a severe supply squeeze. Prices for ammonium paratungstate recently climbed to record highs of US$318.50 (A$448.50) per metric tonne unit, with one MTU equal to 10 kilograms of material.



The sharp run-up in prices has thrust Viking’s Nevada assets into sharper focus as Western supply chains hunt for secure, reliable tungsten sources. In a bid to fast-track early cash flow and capitalise on record prices, the company has started quantifying historical above-ground stockpiles and material within a sizeable tailings dam. The stockpiles are now being tested to confirm the high-grade potential of this low-cost feed source, building on earlier due diligence samples collected late last year that returned 0.8 per cent tungsten trioxide. In parallel with the stockpile assessment, Viking has launched a grid-sampling program across the project’s tailings dam to estimate its volume, tonnage and potential economic value as an additional feed source for immediate processing or toll treatment. With tungsten increasingly recognised as a strategic metal critical to defence, industrial tooling and high-performance alloys, Linka is shaping as a timely project in a prime jurisdiction.



If maiden drilling delivers and early economics stack up, Viking’s Linka tungsten project in Nevada could soon evolve into a serious new tungsten contender. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au
